title: Security Awareness Program
objective: By the end of this lesson you can design a awareness program that changes behavior, run phishing simulations that teach instead of punish, and grow a reporting culture you can measure.

blocks.text: Why people are an interface, not a weakness

Attackers reach people through email, phone calls, text messages, and chat apps because people are reachable. A security awareness program treats staff as a sensor network: thousands of employees who can spot and report an attack in seconds, if they know what to look for and who to tell. The exam words this as recognition-based training: teach people to recognize what an attack looks like rather than memorize rules.

items: Role-appropriate training: everyone gets phishing and data handling basics; developers get secure coding; administrators get privileged access practices.
Regular cadence: short monthly or quarterly reinforcement instead of one annual slide deck that everyone forgets.
Current threat topics: business email compromise, invoice fraud, fake delivery or bank messages, and manipulated voice or video.
Simple reporting channel: one button or one address to report suspicious mail, answered quickly every time.

blocks.text: Phishing simulations send safe fake emails and measure behavior. Good programs start easy, increase difficulty slowly, and pair every click with just-in-time training: a short lesson shown at the teachable moment, not a punishment. Publicly shaming clickers destroys the reporting culture the program exists to build.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Watch for answers that punish users: they are almost always wrong. The best answer usually pairs simulation with immediate training and rewards reporting. When a question describes an employee who clicked and then reported the mail, treat the report as success, because reporting is the behavior you want to grow.

The report rate matters most in the long run. A workforce that reports suspicious mail quickly turns every future campaign into an early-warning system, which is why a rising report rate is celebrated even more than a falling click rate.

blocks.title: Design one campaign month
steps: Pick one audience, for example head office staff, and one theme, for example fake bank alerts.
Write one learning objective, the simulation difficulty, and the just-in-time training a clicker will see.
Choose two metrics from the table above and state the direction you want each to move.
blocks.expected: A workable month looks like: objective is that staff pause at unexpected urgency and check the sender; difficulty starts easy; clickers get a two-minute coaching page; click rate should fall and report rate should rise compared with last quarter.

cheatsheet: Awareness training is recognition-based: teach staff to recognize attacks, then make reporting effortless.
Phishing simulations: start easy, escalate slowly, and pair every click with just-in-time training, never punishment.
A click followed by a report is a success story, not a failure.
Track click rate falling and report rate rising; report rate is the healthiest long-term signal.
Tailor content to roles and to current local scams, and keep sessions short and frequent.

checkpoint.prompt: In a quarterly phishing simulation, an accountant clicks the link, realizes the mistake, and reports the email within two minutes. What is the best reading of this result?

choices.A: The program failed because she clicked
choices.B: The click proves training must be mandatory weekly
choices.C: The click is a miss, but the fast report shows the program is working
choices.D: She should be named in the monthly report so others learn

checkpoint.explanation: The goal is a workforce that recognizes and reports. One click with a two-minute report is a self-correcting event and shows the reporting culture is functioning. Punishment or public naming suppresses future reports.
